stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-02 (Harness durable timeline and event replay). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: The pane dropped 25 of the 43 event types app.py emits, and the walk proves it in a browser: a session created through POST /api/harness/sessions (which makes the server append session/init) drew an empty trajectory before this story and now draws a card - `every held event draws a card, so session/init is no longer a blank trajectory - cards=1 held=1`. The counts are the server's: `harness_timeline_inventory.py` parses the types out of the _append_harness_event/_safe_append_harness_event call sites (43) and out of the renderer (18 with a card), and 18 + 25 = 43 with no type left in between.

`renderStoredHarnessEventHtml()` now ends in `renderRecordedHarnessEventHtml(ev)`, so a type with no card arrives as a compact line read from the event (`session/init  standard policy · direct /tmp/... · lead Qwen3.8-27B`, `security/policy_revision  standard -> plan (revision 2)`, `edit/applied  applied · src/app.py`). The inventory fails on `renderer_ends_in_the_fallback`, on any `return ""` in the renderer, and on a card for a type nothing emits (`no_dead_branches`) - a dead branch is a card no event can reach.

The strip states what the trajectory is: `following the log from seq 13 · 13 events held · replayed 3 times` while the stream fills it, `1 event held, seq 1-1 · cursor 1 of 1` after a page read with the stream closed, `the log did not resume (events_pruned), so this view is the snapshot's: task state and 9 events, seq 5-13` when the fallback fired, and `· 4 earlier events pruned, retained from seq 5 · this view holds 9 of the 13 events last reported` for a pruned or incomplete view. Every one of those sentences is produced by harnessLogState() from the log it holds and the last page it read, not from prose; the walk reads each one out of the DOM.

The reader's place survives a frame. `harnessStreamNearBottom()` (28px slack, the chat transcript's rule) is consulted once before the transcript is rewritten: a pinned view follows, and a reading view keeps its `scrollTop` and its open `<details>` cards - the walk scrolls to 0, replays, and reads `scrollTop 0 -> 0`. Jump to latest is drawn only when the reader is away from the newest event (`hidden at bottom=true shown when up=true`), and pressing it is what returns them (`hidden after=true atBottom=true`). The walk asks the browser for pixels, not for the `hidden` property, because `.btn` sets its own display and had made the first version of the button always visible.

Replay rebuilds from the record: `replayHarnessLog()` empties the cache, re-reads the log from its first retained event and re-renders from what came back - `before=13 after=13 cards=13`, twice, with `replayed 1 time` then `replayed 2 times`, so a replay is countable and a duplicate is impossible (the seq-keyed merge is untouched). A replay that hits a gap does not pretend: it records the reason, says so, and resyncs the authoritative snapshot instead.

The engine underneath is unchanged: the six gap reasons (no_page, snapshot_required, cursor_ahead, events_pruned, sequence_gap, missing_events), seq-deduplication, the cursor, snapshot_required handling, the pruned-history notice, the three stream frames (task_event, resync_required, stream_error) and the resync path that re-reads /state and re-anchors the stream all still work, and the inventory fails if any of them goes. No endpoint was added: the strip reads the four routes the pane already had.

The strip is capped at 45% of the pane and its list at min(168px, 22vh), and it does not shrink away: at 1440x560 the walk measures the strip keeping its line and the trajectory keeping its floor. The hidden Jump button is not drawn either - a `[hidden]` rule for `.btn` inside the strip, because `.btn`'s own display beat the UA rule and the first build showed a control that was not offered.

visual_evidence.shows: The Harness at 1440x900 with a newly created session: the Session log strip saying `1 event held, seq 1-1 · cursor 1 of 1`, opened to its single row `#1 session/init · standard policy · direct /tmp/m5-demo-.../workspace · lead Qwen3.8-27B`, and below it the card that row points at - the session that used to draw an empty trajectory.

The same session after twelve policy changes: `13 events`, `following the log from seq 13 · 13 events held · replayed 3 times`, rows #1 session/init, #2 standard -> plan (revision 2), #3 plan -> autonomous (revision 3)..., Replay and Resync in the bar, and the recorded-event cards in the trajectory matching the rows one for one.

A log whose head was pruned: the strip in its warning colour reading `9 events held`, `4 earlier events pruned, retained from seq 5`, `this view holds 9 of the 13 events last reported`, with the rows starting at #5 because that is all the pane can show.
The same state at 1440x560, where the strip and the trajectory compete for room: the strip keeps its line and the trajectory keeps enough of the pane to read.

decisions: The strip is a view of what the browser holds, not a second log. It states the count it has, the range it covers, the cursor it is at and the newest seq the last page reported; it never claims to know an event it does not hold, which is why the widest sentence it can write about missing history is `this view holds 9 of the 13 events last reported`.

Unknown event types get a recorded-event card rather than a nicer one per type. The point of the story is that nothing is dropped, and a card per type would grow a 43-branch renderer that rots; `harnessEventSummary()` describes the 25 types in the reader's terms and the card prints whatever the event carries for anything newer.

A gap is never smoothed over. If the log will not resume, the strip's first clause says so and names the reason, and the view is described as the snapshot's - the same rule the resync toast already followed, moved from a transient toast into the surface it describes.

Place is preserved rather than restored after the fact: the renderer asks `harnessStreamNearBottom()` once, before rewriting, and a reading view keeps its `scrollTop` and its open cards. Jump to latest exists because a reader who is behind has no other way back without hunting for the bottom.
Pruning wins the strip's colour over the live/replay tone, because a missing event matters more than whether the view is live; the sentence still says both.

The frontend changed, so the source manifest, route map, authorization trace, control inventory, tokens, status components, overlays, onboarding, presentations, studio.py and the preservation package were all regenerated in this branch.

stories.title: Harness approval safety and permission UX
stories.description: Incrementally implement harness approval safety and permission ux using current code as authoritative baseline.
stories.current_behavior: Approving a Harness tool call is not "run it once": POST /api/harness/approve resolves the gate and _persist_approval_grant_outcome() records a scoped grant under the approval's own id - one use, the exact arguments, issued_by=operator_approval, ten minutes by default - and check_revocation_denials() is what refuses it after a revocation. The pane said none of it. An approval arrived as one of four different cards (the streamed card, appendWorkflowApprovalCard, updateWorkflowApprovalCard and the GSD/Turn path), three of which printed a hardcoded "Standard Policy" badge whatever policy was in force; the streamed card posted activeHarnessId as the session while the other two posted d.session_id; no card stated the capability or the resource scope the decision would record, none said how long the record lasted, expiry was drawn only after the fact, and nothing could list or revoke what an approval had left behind even though the grants routes existed.
stories.target_behavior: An approval states the permission it records before the click - the policy asking, the tool, the exact arguments, the capability and resource, the one-use limit and the minute it expires - and the decision is sent with the session that owns it; refusing says what it does instead; an offer nobody answered reads as expired with the next step; and the session's permissions, revocation rules, history and pending approvals are inspectable and revocable from the pane, with a revocation that says the rule it creates outlives the grant, because it does.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-03 (Harness approval safety and permission UX). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: Four paths could raise an approval and each drew its own card; three printed the same hardcoded `Standard Policy` badge whatever policy was in force. `renderHarnessApprovalCardHtml()` is now the only builder and all four paths draw with it, and the policy it prints is the option's own label from `#harnessPolicy` (`harnessPolicyLabel()`), so the card and the select cannot describe one policy two ways. The inventory fails if a second headline, a second decision control or a policy literal comes back.

The card states what the click records, in the units the store uses: tool, exact arguments, capability (`scoped_grants.resolve_tool_capabilities()`), resource, and `one use · 10 minutes after you decide`. The capability line is a client table that this story's inventory imports the real function to check - 18 tools and the `mcp__*` rule - so the copy is verified rather than trusted, and the ttl it prints is compared with `SG_DEFAULT_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS`. The resource line names the path argument it can see and says where the server will resolve it; the surface prints the canonical `path:<worktree>:<rel>` from the record, so the pane never invents a scope it did not receive.

The old streamed card posted `activeHarnessId` and the workflow cards posted `d.session_id`, which is how a stale card could earn a 403. Every path now passes the session it drew with, `resolveHarnessApproval()` falls back to the selected session only when the card carried none, and the walk captures the `POST /api/harness/approve` body to prove `session_id` is the seeded session.

Expiry is stated while the offer is live: the card counts down from the request (`expires in 9 min`, then seconds), one interval drives every live card and clears itself when the last one is gone, and an offer whose slot is gone reads `Expired — re-run the turn` with `Re-run the turn to reach the gate again` - not as a refusal, because nothing was refused. A decided card keeps its arguments: the resolved event carries only `{approval_id, decision, note, step}`, so the request is filed in `harnessApprovalRequests` when it is first drawn and the decided card is redrawn from it.

The permissions surface (`#harnessGrantsModal`, opened by `#harnessPermissionBadge` in the session strip and by `Permissions & Revocations` in the session actions) lists what the session holds with tool, capability, canonical resource, limit, expiry, `issued_by` and note; the revocation rules that refuse matching actions; the history of grants that ended and how; and the approvals still waiting (with a link to the card) or expired. A failed read says it failed instead of drawing an empty session, a slow read is dropped when the reader has selected another session, and the badge says `No permissions` in words.

Revoking is two steps and says what it does: that the grant stops, that a revocation rule refuses the capability on the scope for the rest of the session, that matching running commands are stopped too, and that neither can be undone from here. That last sentence is the one the story had to get right - the store permits issuing a fresh grant after a revocation (verified against the live API before this story), so only `check_revocation_denials()` stops the action, and the confirmation says so rather than offering an undo that does not exist.

The walk could not ask the API for an approval, because no route mints one: `_PENDING_APPROVALS` is in-process state written only when a running turn reaches the gate, and the demo has no runtime. `scripts/harness_permissions_seed.py` therefore boots the ordinary isolated demo environment and calls the app's own `_create_pending_tool_approval()` twice and lets one slot lapse the way the runtime does. The approvals, grants and events are the server's own records; only the arrival is staged, and the fixture says so in its own docstring.

visual_evidence.shows: An approval before any decision at 1440x900: the policy in force (`Standard (Ask before Bash)`, the option's own label), `step 3`, `run_bash` with the exact command, `Capability code_execution, workspace_read, workspace_write`, `Resource this session's worktree, and nothing outside it`, `Limit one use · 10 minutes after you decide`, the expiry clock with a live countdown, the sentence that approving records a one-use permission for this exact call and is not a standing allow, and the two decision controls.

An offer nobody answered: the card is drawn at 0.82 opacity with no decision buttons, and says `This request was never decided — the run it belonged to ended. Re-run the turn to reach the gate again; nothing was granted.`

The permissions surface opened from the badge: `hns-c5a74e19 · policy Standard (Ask before Bash) · revision 1`, the grant the approval recorded under the approval id itself with its canonical `workspace:/tmp/m5-demo-.../workspace` scope, `one use · exact arguments only`, `9 min left` and `operator_approval`, and the expired offer beneath it.

The same surface after a two-step revoke: `This session holds no permission. 1 revocation rule refuses matching actions anyway.`, the rule `blocks code_execution, workspace_write` on that workspace for the rest of the session, and the grant in the history as `revoked — operator_revoked` with no countdown left to mislead.

decisions: One card builder, four call sites. The alternative - keeping four renderers and adding the missing sentences to each - is what let three of them print a policy badge that was not the policy in force.

The capability line is a client table checked against `scoped_grants.resolve_tool_capabilities()` by the inventory rather than a value read from the server, because the server records the grant only after the decision. The resource line names the argument and says where it will be resolved, because the pane cannot canonicalise a path the way the server does and should not pretend to.
The ttl printed on the card is `SG_DEFAULT_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS`; the pane does not offer a per-decision ttl. A duration chosen in the browser would be a second policy beside the one the server stamps.

The rights surface offers revocation per grant, not by capability or scope. `POST /grants/revoke` supports the second form, and exposing it would create a rule that refuses actions no card on screen names.

The revocation confirmation says the rule cannot be undone from here, because the store keeps revocation rules for the life of the session and re-issuing the capability does not clear one. The pane does not offer an undo the server does not have.

The walk seeds its approvals with `scripts/harness_permissions_seed.py` rather than adding a route: the story's contract is that no endpoint is added, and a dev-only mint endpoint would be a privilege the product does not have.

Three test files had nine written into them; they are updated to ten rather than made to accept any number, because a count that cannot fail cannot catch an overlay that stops being tracked. The sign-off test's two route totals are re-derived from the route map, because they move whenever a call site is added and were pinning the previous frontend.

The approve route, the grant store, the revoke semantics and the denial checks are untouched. The unshallowed clone was needed for `verify_baseline.py`; that is an environment step, not a code change.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-04 (Harness verification diff and artifacts). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: A verdict used to be a label. `turn/verified` drew `Completion verified (spec_sha256…)` - the digest of a contract the reader could not see - and `turn/verification_failed` drew a failure code and a reason, while the transcript, the exit code, the revision, the classification and the acceptance coverage that decided it stayed in the log. A third outcome, `turn/stagnation_paused`, was not drawn as a verdict at all. `renderHarnessVerdictCardHtml()` now draws all three from the report the runtime persisted (`TaskVerificationReport.to_dict()` is the event payload): the contract digest, the command with its exit code and classification, the revision the result is tied to and whether it moved, the modified files, the patch digest, the environment, the failing tests with their kind, the covered and uncovered criteria, and the output behind a disclosure. The inventory fails if a second verdict renderer appears or the one-line label comes back.

The card never invents a value the record does not hold: a report with no captured revision says `no revision captured`, one whose command never executed says `the verification command never ran`, and the card ends with `A verdict is the runtime's record of one turn: this card draws it, and re-runs nothing`. The inventory breaks both fallbacks in a copy of the source to prove they are checked.

The record behind the card is `#harnessEvidenceModal`, reached from the session actions (`Verification & Artifacts`), the command palette, every verdict card and the diff dialog. It reads only routes that already existed - `GET …/task` and `GET …/diff` - and draws six sections: the verdict (code, facts, failures, evidence refs, transcript digest, output), the contract (command, first stage, required output markers, required and modified files, protected digests, baseline digests, the rules in force, known failures, declared criteria), the observation (exit code, classification, pre-existing failures classified as pre-existing, output digest, and the coverage the transcript actually demonstrated), the change (branch, status, per-file +n/-m), the artifacts (checkpoints, the latest checkpoint's evidence refs, the artifact lineage, the revision a re-run would be tied to), and four statements of what the surface does not prove. No endpoint was added; the inventory fails on an invented or unmounted verification route.

Coverage is drawn as what the transcript printed, not as what the contract hoped: `evaluate_acceptance_coverage()` counts a test id only when it appears in the output and is not among the classified failures, so an uncovered criterion is drawn `NOT COVERED` and counted (`1 declared criterion(s) were not covered by an observed test`). The contract section draws the same criteria as `declared` with no verdict mark, because the contract is the gate and the observation is what happened when it was applied - a first pass drew them as uncovered there and the walk caught the contradiction.

Three absences are drawn as absences, proved in the walk: no verdict in the log (`No verdict is recorded in this session's log yet`), no contract on the session (`This session has no verification contract, so completion was not gated by one`), and an unreadable diff (`The workspace diff could not be read`). None is drawn as a pass; the walk selects a seeded session that has a contract and no verdict and asserts both that no card is drawn and that the record's verdict block carries no tone.

The change is counted once. `harnessDiffFiles()` parses the unified diff, skipping `diff --git`, `+++`, `---` and `@@` so a hunk header cannot be read as an addition, and both the record and `#harnessDiffModal` count with it - the dialog now shows `1 file(s) · +1 −1 · on master` above the diff and says `This is the worktree as it is now. It is not frozen at any verdict`. The parser is exercised against output real `git` produced in a temporary repository, not a hand-written sample.

The fixture cannot fake a verdict: only `TaskStateMachine.verify_task_completion()` produces a report, and the demo has no model runtime. `scripts/harness_evidence_seed.py` therefore builds two git workspaces, sets a real `TaskVerificationSpec` on each session, and lets that verifier decide - one workspace passes its test, one fails it - then appends the reports with `_append_harness_event()`, the writer a turn uses, and records a checkpoint with the store's own `save_checkpoint()`. What is staged is the `turn/start` and `turn/end` bookends; the revision, environment, exit code, transcript digest, classified failures and coverage are the verifier's.

The diff, apply and task contracts are unchanged and checked: `_compute_git_diff()` still redacts (`combined = redact_text(`), bounds the payload at 50 000 characters and previews untracked files, `/apply` still refuses a read-only policy and reports a quarantined workspace, and `/task` still returns the spec, the evidence preview, the checkpoints and the lineage - the inventory fails if any of those checks stop seeing what they look for, and a test breaks each one in a copy of `app.py`.

decisions: The surface reads `GET …/task` and `GET …/diff` and adds no route. Both carried everything the story needed - the contract and the read-only evidence preview were already in the task view, and the diff was already in the diff route - so the story is a pane change, and the inventory fails if a verification endpoint appears that the server does not mount.

The verdict is drawn from the durable event payload rather than from a new record: `turn/verified`, `turn/verification_failed` and `turn/stagnation_paused` already carry `TaskVerificationReport.to_dict()`, so the card reads the same fields the log holds and a resync repaints it without a second source of truth.

A declared acceptance criterion is drawn as `declared` in the contract section and as `covered`/`not covered` only in the observation, because a contract is a promise and coverage is a measurement. The first implementation judged coverage in both places; the walk showed the same criterion reading `NOT COVERED` in the contract and `covered` in the observation, and the renderer was split rather than the wording patched.

The diff dialog gained a per-file summary and an honesty note instead of a second diff view: one parser (`harnessDiffFiles()`) counts the change for both the dialog and the record, so the two cannot disagree about how many files moved.

The walk's verdicts are produced by the product's own verifier on two real git workspaces, because a hand-written report would prove only that the pane can render JSON. What is staged is the turn's arrival; the reports are `TaskStateMachine.verify_task_completion()`'s own output.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-05 (Harness pause cancel resume and crash recovery UX). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: A run that stopped used to be one line in the log. `turn/paused` drew `Paused at step 4 - operator_pause_requested`, `turn/cancelled` drew `Cancelled - operator_cancelled`, `turn/resume_prepared` drew a next step, and none of them said what had survived, what it would cost to go on, or what a reader could press. The four routes built for exactly this moment - `POST …/pause`, `…/cancel`, `…/resume`, `…/contain` - were reachable from the API and from nowhere in the pane, whose only control was Abort: an action that ends the view, not the work. A worker that died left the task saying `running` with no stream attached, and the pane drew that as a running task.

`#harnessRecoveryPanel` sits under the session strip and above the durable log, and is one presentation - so it cannot be drawn without a cause and a `Kept:` line - over a facts list and a live note. It reads only what the server already returns: `GET …/state` (status, transitions, checkpoints, budget, turns) and `GET …/task` (task record, recovery memory, containment store, budget). Every fact on it is one of those fields. No route was added.

Seven states, each with its own story: paused at a safe boundary (the transition's own reason, printed beside a plain phrase, and the checkpoint a resume restarts from); failed (with the requirement for changed evidence); blocked (the unresolved action by id, resume refused, cancel offered); cancelled (what was fenced and revoked, and that no resume exists); running and owned by this pane (a pause lands at the next safe boundary); running and not owned by this pane (the record cannot tell another tab's run from a dead worker, and the surface says so instead of guessing); and a resume the runtime accepted, drawn as `prepared` with `nothing has run yet` rather than as progress. A completed task draws no surface at all.

The presses are the real routes: Pause (`POST …/pause`, and a deferred pause says it is deferred), Resume (`POST …/resume`), Continue (`/api/harness/run` with `resume: true`, only after an accepted resume), Cancel (`POST …/cancel`, behind a confirmation that any other action disarms), Abort (the existing `/abort`, which now says it ends the view and not the work) and Start a new session. A press that reaches the server prints the answer it got - including the string `detail` a rejected transition carries and the `{code, message}` a rejected handoff carries.

Every reason a resume would be refused is computed from the same record before the press - the task state, a failed checkpoint integrity check, unresolved consequential actions, a persisted barrier, a pending cancellation, an exhausted budget, a quarantine, unreadable recovery memory - and the action stays visible and disabled with the reason as its accessible description and the same reason in text (`Not available here — …`). `presentInto()` grew `disabled`, `reason` and a `tone` for destructive actions so a refusal could be drawn instead of hidden.

The three recovery events are one card renderer now, saying what the event did (`0 in-flight process(es) were contained`, `2 consequential action(s) were left unresolved …`) and linking back to the surface that keeps saying it after the log scrolls past.

The one capability the pane could never exercise even with the routes reachable: `/api/harness/run` accepts `resume` and the pane never sent it, so a resume the runtime had accepted was followed by a turn that started over at step 1. The request now carries the flag when a resume is prepared, and consumes the preparation in that request.

`scripts/uiux_harness_recovery_inventory.py`: 44 checks over the markup, the seven stories, the six actions, the eleven refusals, the three event cards, the escaping of every value the record supplies and the seven server contracts this story had to preserve (pause's `deferred_to_safe_boundary`, cancel's `unresolved_action_ids`/`contained_processes`, resume's `ready_to_resume`/`next_step`, containment's quarantine and barrier holds, `/task`'s recovery and containment, `/state`'s `task_status` and `transitions`, and the absence of any new recovery route). 0 findings.

`scripts/harness_recovery_walk.mjs`: 23/23 checks in a real browser against `scripts/harness_recovery_seed.py`, which drives `ensure_root_task`, `transition_task`, `save_checkpoint`, `request_pause`, `cancel_task` and a real `persist_barrier_hold()` into paused / blocked / cancelled / was-running states, then presses the pane's own controls against the real routes. It proves the prepared-resume answer, the two-press cancel, the disabled refusal, that the server's own 409 agrees with the reason the surface stated, that a reason which is markup is drawn as text (no element, no handler), that focus survives an action, that a run started after a prepared resume sends `resume: true`, and that every request the surface made was one of the four routes that already existed. No page error.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-06 (Pipeline stages dependencies and artifacts). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: The four seats are a chain - the architect writes a spec, the builder is handed it, the critic is handed both, the judge is handed all three - and that chain lived only in `api_council_stream`'s input lambdas. The pane drew four cards carrying a state and a tok/s, so a finished run could not answer the two questions a pipeline raises: what did each seat receive, and what did it hand on? A seat that produced nothing looked exactly like a seat that had just started, and a run that was stopped looked like a run that was still going.

Every stage card now carries two rows. The handoff row names what the seat reads (`the task + the Architect's spec and the Builder's draft`), the characters of upstream output it was handed, and the seat it feeds (or `ends the run` for the judge); the artifact row states what it produced - characters, tokens, tok/s, the reasoning it kept - or `produced nothing` with the empty section the next seat was handed. The collapsed step card carries its seat's character count, and `#councilArtifacts` above the cards is one live run line: how many seats finished, the total output, the handoffs that carried content forward, and whether the server saved the run.

The chain is mirrored in `PIPELINE_SEATS` and checked against `app.py` on every inventory run: the pane's copy is compared with the `c['...']` reads in each stage's input lambda, so a mirror that drifts is a failing check rather than a quiet lie.

What the surface refuses to claim is stated on it. The sizes count this pane's own stream, not the prompt the server assembles around them, and the page says so. `save_run()` is called after the fourth seat returns and returns `0` when it cannot write, so a stopped pipeline is drawn as stopped and is never given a run id; a run that finished without one says its artifacts exist only on this screen. No endpoint was added to read a saved run back: `/api/runs` does not exist and this story did not create it.

The empty seat was staged, not invented: `scripts/pipeline_artifacts_seed.py` wraps the server's own `stream_any_model` so one model arrives with usage and no content and another streams slowly enough to Stop. The events, the character counts and the run id are the server's answers.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P3-07 (Pipeline retry failure and checkpoint recovery). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: A run that failed was a toast: `Council error: HTTP 503` for four seconds, then nothing. The seat it died on was not named, the output that had survived was not named, and there was no record anywhere - `save_run()` writes a run only after the fourth seat returns - so reloading the page threw away the only copy, and the only way to try again was to retype the task, which may not have been the task that failed.

`#pipelineRecovery` is one block under the run line, built by `presentInto()`, so it cannot ship without a title, a cause, a `Kept:` line and at least one action. It draws six states from what happened: a seat that failed (named, with the provider's own message, the characters that survived and the note that nothing is on record), a run the operator stopped, a stream that ended without the run's final event, a run read back from this browser's checkpoint, a run read back from the server's export, and a finished run announcing the id the server saved.

Retry re-posts the payload the run was started with instead of re-reading the controls, and says that the server has no single-seat entry point, so all four seats run again; the run line then says which attempt it is drawing. The salvage is written to `localStorage` before the page can go away (capped at 60,000 characters, truncated per seat and said to be truncated), offered after a reload rather than drawn, restored without re-running anything, and never described as the server's record. A run that was saved is read back through `GET /api/history/export` - the bundle an operator can already download, which redacts credentials - and a run that was not saved is never given an id.

Three endings are three states: `failed`, `stopped` and `dropped`, each with its own title and cause, so a failure no longer reads as a stop. A seat that was left mid-stream stops claiming to be streaming or connecting: the card says `Stopped`, the pill says `Stopped mid-seat`, and the artifact row says what it stopped after instead of `produced so far`.

No endpoint was added: `/api/runs` still does not exist, and the only route this story calls is the export that already existed. The council route, its seven events, its run record, `save_run()`'s ordering and the shared stream reader are pinned by the inventory.

evidence: The Council pane had four pickers and no answers: it could not say what a seat was for, and it could not say whether the model in a picker was resident, loadable, reachable, or missing an API key. On a machine whose local runtime was down, every local seat was answered by `_stream_omlx_completion`'s canned demo text while the transcript drew a tok/s badge for text no model produced, and a seat that failed said so in a four-second toast while its card went on saying "Connecting...".

Each of the four seats now carries its role - the server's own `AGENT_ROLES` label (Staff Architect, Fast Coder / Analyst, Adversarial Critic, Lead Arbiter), which the pane keeps in one map and applies to the transcript card from the `role_key` the summon route already stored - plus one line saying what the seat is for and one verdict read from `GET /api/telemetry` and `GET /api/providers`: `READY` with the memory a resident model holds, `NEEDS LOAD` / `NEEDS MEMORY` with the gigabytes it needs against the ceiling and what is left, `NEEDS KEY` for an alias saved without one, `NOT LISTED` for a model the runtime does not serve, `DEMO TEXT` when the runtime is not answering at all, `NO MODEL` when the picker is empty, and `UNVERIFIED` when telemetry has not answered. Each non-ready row offers the one action that exists - load it, open the providers panel, or move focus to the picker - and every row is described by an `evidenceNote` basis that names both reads and how old they are.

The rows and the round read one `hallSeatPlan()`, so a row cannot describe a seat the dispatch would not post; the plan keeps the old fallback chain (the seat's picker, then the Pipeline's picker for the same seat, then the catalogue default). A combo is judged by its targets rather than by existing, so a combo of local models on a dead runtime is demo text. The summary counts the rows and says the round stops at the first seat that fails, because `runHallFullRound` breaks there.

The demo path's usage line now carries `demo: true`, so a reply the server wrote itself is labelled a demo reply and is not given the tok/s badge it did not earn. A failed seat is a `presentInto()` block naming the seat, quoting the provider, stating that nothing was saved for that model, with Retry / Check readiness / Ask one model, and the server's transcript is redrawn first so no card keeps claiming to connect.

No endpoint was added: the only route the story calls is `POST /api/models/{model_id:path}/load`, which the Residency panel already used, and the route map now records the new caller as a certain one. The summon route's four events, its defaults, `append_hall_message`'s usage column, and the four seat pickers are pinned by the inventory.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P4-02 (Council deliberation stages and evidence). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: A council stage card drew a state, a tok/s and a character count and never said the ceiling the count was measured against, so a seat that spent its whole token budget read exactly like one that answered in three hundred tokens. The reasoning control offered three modes for "the run" while `api_council_stream` gave them to seats 1 and 4 only, the Critic was deliberately written without the skill playbook and nothing said so, and the handoff row counted `content` alone while `WorkflowOrchestrator.run_stages` hands the next seat `result.content or result.reasoning` - so a seat that answered in thinking only read as `0 chars`, exactly like a seat that answered nothing.

`stage_start` now publishes the contract a seat runs under - `max_tokens`, `reasoning_mode`, and the application's own `meta` (`skills`) through a new `WorkflowStage.meta` - and every stage card draws it in a `.stage-contract` row: budget, reasoning mode, skills decision, plus a verdict chip when the reply was cut or written by the server. The pane keeps that from the event (`stageBuffers[stage].k`) and holds no copy: an inventory check fails if a budget literal appears in `static/index.html`.

What a seat carries forward is now `content or reasoning` on all four surfaces that describe it - the handoff row, the artifact row, the run line and the evidence table - so an empty output that handed on a reasoning trace reads as exactly that, and an empty section is only claimed when there was nothing to hand on. The reasoning select says which seats it reaches, and the route and the label name the same two.

`#deliberationEvidence` states one row per seat - allowed, given, produced, carried, verdict - drawn with the cards from the same run, redrawn only when a value in it changes, keeping the focus on its one control across the redraw, and **Copy evidence** writes the same table as markdown. Six verdicts and none drawn as another: `answered`, `capped` (the runtime's own length limit and this run's budget are named separately), `demo text`, `no output`, `streaming`, `not run`.

The Council pane no longer prints a throughput figure for demo text anywhere: the stage card's pill, the stepper's meta and the artifact row all say what the reply was instead of the 29.5/42.1 tok/s the demo path fabricated. The numbers still reach `perf_samples` (see the P4-01 open risk) - this story removed the drawing, not the write, and says so.

The fixture can now produce the states the story is about: `scripts/council_readiness_seed.py` gained `--cap-model` (a reply ending in `finish_reason: "length"`) and `--reasoning-model` (a reply streamed as `reasoning_content` only). `scripts/council_deliberation_walk.mjs` drives the real `/api/council/stream` against it, reads the contract rows, the handoff rows and the table out of the DOM, puts focus on the copy control and lets a whole run redraw the table under it, then repeats on the offline fixture (14 checks).

No endpoint was added and the stream's seven events are unchanged: the evidence is read from what the route already sent. `scripts/uiux_pipeline_artifacts_inventory.py` (P3-06) was widened, not silenced - its rule now reads the `stage_start` fields that carry the skills decision instead of forbidding the claim outright.
The tree this closes is fcbfcd3d702ea820add0204f0bd5a79f60e0c407: recorded here rather than in that commit, because a commit cannot carry its own sha.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P4-03 (Council consensus disagreement and results). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: The Hall could draw a transcript, and - if a seat had been asked for its verdict - a banner whose only claim was `Pinned Council Conclusion (author)`. So nothing said what that decision had to do with the four replies above it, whether four seats had produced four readings or one reading four times, or that a session ending with nothing pinned had settled nothing. A result is now a stated thing rather than a blob of prose.

`#hallVerdict` sits under the pinned conclusion and states the decision's provenance: the reply it came from, matched on the author the server recorded *and* the words it kept (`hallVerdictDecision`), with the time it was pinned and the sentence `one seat's reply as written; it is not a synthesis of the others`. A conclusion written by a human through `POST /api/hall/sessions/{id}/close` is drawn as `pinned by <author>` and credited to no seat. The decision text itself still draws in `#hallConclusionBanner`, unchanged.

Every other reply is measured against the decision by **shared wording**: the fraction of its 4-word sequences that also appear in the decision - containment rather than Jaccard, because a short reply carried by a long decision should read as carried - with single words for a reply shorter than four. The thresholds are 0.85 / 0.70 / 0.25 and the readings are `is the decision`, `mostly in the decision`, `partly in the decision`, `not in the decision`; the block publishes the arithmetic in its own basis line and says `It measures text, not intent`.

Dissent is named, counted and left where it is: replies under 25 % are listed under **Dissent** with their percentage and the line `Each stays in the transcript above, as written`. The verdict block writes nothing into `#hallStream` - an inventory check fails if it touches it - so no reply is merged, summarised or re-worded, and a session with nothing pinned says `no decision pinned` and `nothing has been settled`.

The pane counts voices, not replies. With nothing pinned the same measure runs between replies, grouped greedily at 0.85 in transcript order, and the headline reads `N replies · M voices`; a group of identical answers is named (`Seat 1 and Seat 4 (100 %)`) with the sentence `A result that counted replies would call this consensus; it is the same answer, repeated`. On the offline fixture, where the server writes the same demo text for every seat, the block reads `4 replies · 1 voice` instead of presenting four identical replies as a council that agrees.

A seat that answered twice is told apart: the Arbiter replies in the round and again for its verdict, so rows carry `(reply 2)` when a seat spoke more than once, and the decision is credited to the later reply rather than the first one whose text happens to match. `Copy verdict` writes the same table - columns, percentages, readings and the dissent line - as markdown.

`scripts/council_readiness_seed.py` now answers each catalogue model with its own paragraph (`_reply_words`), because a verdict needs four replies that can be told apart - while two seats pointed at one model still produce identical text, which is the failure the block exists to name. `--offline` is unchanged: every seat is still the server's demo text.

One surface, one payload: the block reads `activeHallData` and calls no route, so the walk's request log shows only `/api/hall/sessions` and `/api/hall/sessions/{id}/summon`. It keeps a per-state signature, so a redraw during a stream does not rewrite an unchanged table or move the focus off its copy control.

Shared wording is a lexical measure: a seat that makes the same point in different words reads as `not in the decision` and is named under Dissent. decisions: The decision's provenance is matched on the author the server recorded *and* the words it kept. An author match alone would credit a conclusion that was edited after pinning (`close_council` can rewrite the text); a text match alone would credit the first seat that happened to say the same thing, which two seats on one model do by construction.

Shared wording is containment of a reply's 4-word sequences in the compared text, not Jaccard: the question is `is this reply carried by that text`, and Jaccard would punish a short reply for the decision's length. The size and the thresholds are constants in the pane and an inventory check fails if the size is hidden.

Voices are grouped greedily in transcript order at 0.85 containment rather than clustered: it is deterministic, explainable to a reader (`the same words as Seat 3`) and stable across redraws, and a transitive cluster would join two replies that never share words through a third.

Dissent is defined as under 25 % containment and documented as a text threshold, not a stance. The block names the percentage and keeps the reply where it was, which is the only reading of `never averaged away` that survives contact with a pane that cannot read intent.

No route was added and no server behaviour changed for the verdict: the block is a view of the session payload the pane already loads, so the cursor, the pin path and the close path are untouched. The one server-side change is the fixture's per-model reply text, which is test tooling.
The verdict block is drawn after `#hallConclusionBanner`, so the decision is read first and measured second. The banner keeps its own rendering rather than being replaced by the block.

stories.title: Compare criteria and side-by-side results
stories.description: Incrementally implement compare criteria and side-by-side results using current code as authoritative baseline.
stories.current_behavior: Before this story the Compare pane was checkboxes, a question and a wall of cards whose only signal was that tokens were arriving. Nothing said what the comparison was being judged on. A panel that failed raised a toast and left its card saying 'Streaming'; a comparison the reader stopped left the same word on screen; the panels behind a failure kept saying 'Waiting' as if their turn were still coming; no row said which models answered, how much they wrote, or whether the runtime had finished the reply or cut it at the length limit; and Start was enabled with no model or no question, where it did nothing but toast.
stories.target_behavior: The Compare pane states what it is comparing and against which criteria before it runs, and reports each model's own status honestly: ten named states read from the response, a run line that counts them, and one results table that reads every model against the criteria while refusing the two it cannot settle (cost, and the reader's own criteria).

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P4-04 (Compare criteria and side-by-side results). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. Never invent a test result.

evidence: `#debateCriteria` is a labelled region above the prompt that names the comparison's criteria before anything runs, because a criterion written after the results exist is a rationalization: three the pane can settle (`Answered at all` from the panel's own reply, `Finished rather than cut` from the response's finish reason, `Size` from the reply the server saved), `Cost` with the reason it is empty (`no price is configured for any model, so this pane claims no money`), and the reader's own criteria (`Correctness`, `Fits my constraints`, add your own) marked `no — yours to judge`. The strip says in its own basis line that three are settled by what the replies and the runtime report and the rest are the reader's.

A panel now has one of ten states - `queued`, `running`, `answered`, `cut at the length limit`, `demo text`, `no reply`, `failed`, `stopped by you`, `stream ended`, `not run` - and each carries a tone from the shared status component. The outcome is read from the response, not from an event having arrived: `usage.demo` makes it demo text, a `finish_reason` of `length` makes it cut, a reply with no words makes it empty, and only a finished reply with words is `answered`. A badge is written per state so `data-tone` stays a literal of the declared vocabulary, and the label still comes from `DEBATE_STATUS` so the two cannot drift.

The endings are attributed. A server error is drawn on the panel that was live (`This panel did not answer: [groq] provider transport failed. Nothing was saved for it.`) and the panels behind it say they never started; Stop marks the live panel `stopped by you`, keeps the partial reply and says what it was; a dropped stream marks it `stream ended`; and the stream's finalizer normalizes anything left `running` or `queued`, so no panel can keep saying it is running after the stream is gone. The old `Streaming`/`Waiting` words are gone from the pane.

`#debateSummary` counts the run in one line (`2 panels · 1 answered · 1 failed`, `1 panel · 1 cut at the length limit`, `1 panel · 1 stopped by you`, `1 panel · 1 demo text`) and carries a `data-state` on the same tones; with nothing run it says `Nothing has been compared yet: choose the models, write the question, then Start Compare.` `#debateResults` is hidden until a panel exists, then states one row per model - model, status, characters, criteria it met - over a footer that refuses the two it cannot settle: `Not settled here: cost (no price is configured for any model) and Correctness, Fits my constraints (yours to judge). This table reports what each reply carried and how it ended - not which reply is better.`

A demo reply is credited with a size and nothing else: the server wrote that text, so it establishes nothing about the model's answering or finishing. A stopped or cut reply is credited with `answered, size` and never `finished`, because it did not finish.

The control that did nothing now says why: `#debateRunBtn` is disabled on the same predicate that writes `#debateRunHint` (`Select at least one model to compare.` / `Write the question to compare on.` / `Ready: 2 models, one question.`), and `runDebate` only toasts when the predicate disagrees with the DOM, which is a bug rather than a path.

One surface, one payload: the pane calls no route it did not call before. The walk's request log shows only `/api/debate/stream`, and the arbiter verdict, Stop, the checkbox list, the skill picker and the judge selector are unchanged and still wired.

Keyboard and pointer: `Enter` in the criterion input adds the criterion through one delegated listener on the strip (an inline `onkeydown` would be a second place the key can be sent from, and `scripts/uiux_chat_inventory.py` fails on it), and the strip re-focuses the input after every add or remove so a reader can type several criteria in a row.

The stream can only say what it can say: `/api/debate/stream` sends one `error` for the whole comparison, because `WorkflowOrchestrator.run_stages` lets a provider exception propagate. The pane attributes that error to the live panel and marks the rest `not run` rather than inventing a per-panel failure; a per-panel event is the orchestrator's change to make. The doc states this limit next to the statuses.

known_regressions: A comparison runs with `auto_unload: true`, so the local model it just compared can leave the catalogue: the checkbox strip is rebuilt from telemetry and stops offering it, while its card and its row stay on screen. The result is honest but confusing on a screenshot, and it is the picker's refresh behaviour (recorded under P4-01) rather than this story's; the walk's captures clip the run line, panels and results for that reason.

The server has no per-panel error event: one provider exception ends the whole `run_stages` run, so a failed comparison always leaves the panels behind it `not run` rather than failing one and carrying on. The pane says exactly that and does not pretend to have a partial panel failure it cannot observe.

Three of the ten states cannot be produced by the app in this environment: `queued` appears only between the click and the first `panel_start`, `empty` needs a runtime that finishes without words, and `stream ended` needs a socket that drops mid-run. They are asserted in the pane's vocabulary and in the inventory, and the fixture can produce six of the ten (answered, cut, demo, failed, stopped, not-run).
decisions: The criteria come first, in the markup and on the page, because a comparison whose criteria are written after the results is reading the results backwards. The three measurable ones name the thing that measures them (`the panel's own reply`, `the response's finish reason`, `the reply the server saved`) so a reader can check the claim.

`cost` is stated and refused rather than omitted: the pane has no price table, so it says `no price is configured for any model, so this pane claims no money`. Cost and provenance (tok/s, tokens, latency read from the response payload rather than the client clock) are UIUX-P4-05's; this story refuses the claim instead of half-making it.

A panel's status is derived from the response, not from the event: `panel_done` alone cannot distinguish a finished reply from one the runtime cut at its length limit or one the server wrote itself, and the demo path exists precisely so a reader is not shown a model's answer where there is none.

A stopped comparison says `stopped by you` and keeps what the panel had written; it does not claim the reply finished, and the criteria column reads `answered, size` for it. Losing the partial text would make Stop useless, and claiming `finished` would make it a lie.

The badge markup is written per state so `data-tone` stays a literal of the six declared tones; the label still comes from `DEBATE_STATUS` so the two cannot drift. A computed `data-tone` hides which tones the pane actually uses from the status-component inventory, which is the artifact that keeps the vocabulary honest.

evidence: `#debateProvenance` sits under the results table and states one row per reply - including the arbiter's - over six columns: model, `elapsed_s`, `ttft`, `completion_tokens` (with `reasoning_tokens` when the reply reasoned), `decode_tps` and cost. Its basis line names the four fields and says `this page times nothing`; the run's own total is `total_elapsed_s` from `debate_done` (`The run took 3.83 s, as the server measured it`).

Every field the pane prints is one `app.py` puts in a `usage` event, and the inventory reads those keys out of `app.py` and fails when the pane reads a field the server does not send. A value the response did not carry is a dash: `debateFigure` returns null for anything missing, non-finite or `<= 0`, and the cell renders `—`, because a zero reads as a measurement and there was none.

No figure comes from the browser. The pane's debate functions call no clock (`performance.now`, `Date.now`, `new Date`, `Date.parse`), and the inventory fails if one appears; the run total comes from the event, not from a timer started at the click. The walk proves the same thing from the other side: it tees the `/api/debate/stream` response, parses the frames the app parses, and compares every cell with the `usage` the server sent for that reply, formatted with the same arithmetic - a client-computed rate could not match a server figure to two decimals.

A demo reply is given no figure at all. The demo path emits `demo: true` with invented numbers (29.5 / 42.1 tok/s decode, 155 tok/s prefill) and `record_perf` still stores them - that write is the runtime program's to remove - so the pane reads the flag and prints five dashes with `demo text: the reply is the server's, so it carries no measured figure`. The walk asserts a demo run's block contains no `tok/s` and neither `29.5` nor `42.1`.

The arbiter's card lost its unqualified badge: `debateArbiterBadge` prints `41.2 tok/s · 0.26 s · 58 tokens` under the title `As the runtime reported it in this reply's usage; this page times nothing.`, says `demo text · no figures` for a demo verdict, and `figures not reported` when the usage carried none. The arbiter's row in the table states the same figures from the same `synthesis_done` usage, and the walk asserts the badge text equals the row's figures.

Cost is stated and refused in the block (`Cost: not known. No price is configured for any model, so no reply here is given one.`) and per row as a dash with that title. The pane reads no price, posts no price route, and still posts only `/api/debate/stream`.

A stage that never reported has a reason, not a blank: `the provider failed before it reported any figure`, `you stopped the run before the runtime reported`, `the stream ended before the runtime reported`, `this panel never started, so nothing was measured`, `the response carried no usage for this panel`. A run that failed claims no total, and the footer says so rather than timing itself.

`scripts/council_readiness_seed.py` gained `--resident-model <id>`: a comparison with two answering panels needs two resident models, and the saved keyless alias fails by design (a failed run never reaches the arbiter, so there would be no verdict to measure). The flag marks an existing catalogue model loaded; `FITS_MODEL` (3.80 GB) still fits under the fixture's 20.8 GB ceiling, and without the flag the fixture is unchanged.
The tree this closes is recorded in `commit_sha`: a commit cannot carry its own sha, so the closeout commit that fills that field is a second commit on the same branch.

stories.agent_prompt: Implement UIUX-P4-06 (Compare saved comparison and export continuity). Verify dependencies, pin HEAD, inventory impacted controls and API routes, preserve all current behavior, make a small compatible change, execute targeted and baseline tests, record screenshots, and mark done only with passing evidence. evidence: `#debateRecord` sits under the measured-performance block and states exactly one of four sources every time it is drawn, as words and as a badge: `live` (`ran on this page` - *the comparison you just ran on this page; a copy is kept in this browser, so a reload restores it*), `browser` (*this browser's copy of the comparison you last ran here · kept at <time> - not the server's record, and not a live run*), `server` (*read back from the server's redacted export; it is the copy on record, not a live run*) and `detached` (*on this page only: this browser is not keeping a copy of it, and a reload will lose it*). Before a run there is no bar at all, because there is nothing to keep.

The save is the server's, and so is the verdict on it: the id comes from `debate_done` (`debateRunId = Number(d.run_id || 0)`, where `save_run` returns 0 on a failed write), so the bar says `The server saved this run as run N; its own copy is in GET /api/history/export` or `The server did not save this run (no run id came back), so the only copy is the one this page holds`. The walk proves both: a two-model run reports run 1, and a run stopped before the server saved it reports 0 and still comes back after its own reload, still `stopped`.

The copy this browser keeps is written when the stream's completion handler runs, so a failed, a stopped and a lost run are kept exactly like a finished one (they are the ones a reader most wants back), under `m5_debate_comparison`, capped at 60,000 characters. Only the longest replies are shortened, the dropped count is recorded in the snapshot, and the bar states it (`N characters of the longest replies were dropped to fit this browser's storage`). A refused write is stated too, not swallowed.

A reload restores the same comparison: the walk reloads, then compares the restored question, the panel count, every card's model and status, the full measured figures, the arbiter and the run id against what was on screen before, and fails on any difference. The restored figures are identical to the exported ones (`The restored comparison is byte-for-byte the one that was exported` compares the markdown minus the source-specific bullet); the restored reply statuses are derived from the same `usage` the server stored (`debateRecordedStatus`: `demo`, `cut` on `finish_reason: length`, else `answered`), so a restored *cut* reply does not come back as *answered*.

A restored comparison cannot pass for a live run - the walk asserts the bar reads `kept in this browser` and not `ran on this page` - and it names the models the current strip no longer offers (`The models this comparison used are not all listed right now (...), so Start would compare something else`), because the model list is live and re-ticking a model the runtime has unloaded would silently compare something else.

The server's own copy is read back through the route that already existed, `GET /api/history/export`, where it sits under `tables.runs`: matched by id and mode `debate`, with the payload's `prompt`, `opinions[].usage`, `synthesis` and `total_elapsed_s` applied through the same `debateApplySnapshot` the browser's copy uses. Because the exporter scrubs credential-shaped strings, the bar and the markdown call it the redacted copy - and the pane posts no new route at all: the walk records every request and sees only `POST /api/debate/stream` and `GET /api/history/export`.

`Forget this copy` removes this browser's key and says what it did not touch (`Forgotten in this browser; the server's record, if any, is untouched`), the bar drops to `detached`/`not kept here`, the Forget control disappears (there is nothing left to forget) and a reload restores nothing - while the server's copy stays readable, which the walk checks by reading it back afterwards.

The comparison leaves the page whole. `Copy as markdown` writes `# Comparison`, the question, one `## Opinion N · <model> · <status>` section per reply, `## Arbiter verdict · <model>`, the `## Measured performance` table and the refusals (`nothing here picks a winner or merges the answers`, `Cost is not stated: no price is configured for any model.`, which copy this is, and whether the server saved it); `Download .json` writes the same comparison as data - one entry per panel with model, status, content and the `usage` the response carried, plus the arbiter, the question, the criteria and the run id. Neither merges the answers, ranks them, or drops the failed and the stopped ones, and a refused clipboard or download is reported instead of silent.

decisions: The bar states a source rather than a boolean `restored` flag. `live`, `browser`, `server` and `detached` are four genuinely different epistemic states, and collapsing them would let a copy read back from a redacted export look like the run the reader performed.

A restored comparison is never re-run automatically and never re-timed: the figures come from the snapshot, the statuses are derived from the stored `usage`, and `debateSource = "live"` is set in exactly one place (`runDebate`), which the inventory pins.

The copy is written in the stream's completion handler, not on success. A failed or stopped comparison is the one a reader most wants back, and P4-04 already established that those states are worth keeping on screen.

The server's copy is read through `GET /api/history/export` rather than a new `/api/debate/runs/{id}` route: the export already carries the run with its usage, it already runs through the redaction path, and a new route would be a new authorization contract for a story that is about continuity, not access.

What the browser keeps is capped and the cap is stated. `localStorage` is small and synchronous; silently keeping a truncated half of a comparison, or throwing when the quota is hit, would both be worse than keeping the most of it and saying what was left out.

The markdown export repeats the refusals the pane makes (`nothing here picks a winner`, cost not stated) rather than only the answers, because an exported comparison is read away from the page that would otherwise have said so.
`Download .json` is a data file, not a report: it carries the raw `usage` per panel so a reader can check every figure, and it names its own source so a file cannot be mistaken for a live run.

evidence: `UI_STATUS` is now the whole vocabulary: one entry per word carrying the label *and* the tone, declared once at the top of the pure-helper region so the node-based tests can reach it too. `uiStatus(state)` throws on a state the table does not know, so an unknown state cannot quietly print itself, and the tone always comes from the same entry - the way a green `running` used to happen was a second map with its own copy of the tone.

The Harness stop inventing words. `HARNESS_STATUS_STATE` maps the server's ten states onto the vocabulary and `harnessStatusBadge()` reads the word and the tone from it, so `FAILED` and `ERROR` are both `failed`, `CANCELLED` is `stopped by you`, `PENDING` is `queued` and `IDLE` is `ready` - four spellings that used to mean two states. A state the table has never seen keeps the server's own word (`something new`) with a neutral tone instead of being mapped onto a word that would be wrong. The session rows in the Harness list and the live badge both call the same function now (`const stIcon = harnessStatusBadge(s).label;`), which is how a row and a badge came to disagree.

The other panes followed: Start's preflight (`Ready`/`Blocked`/`Needs you`) and its health line (`Live`/`Offline`/`Demo data`), the Council readiness count (`0/4 READY`, `NEEDS LOAD`, `NEEDS KEY`), the Council session badge and the container badge (both `.toUpperCase()` of a server word), the pipeline's stage verdicts (`Done`, `Recovered · partial`, `Stopped mid-seat`, `Recovered`, `Unloaded`), the chat tool cards and transcripts (`OK`/`FAILED`, and one call site that said `ERROR`), and the Compare pane's ten states - which were already one vocabulary and are now asserted to *be* this table, word for word and tone for tone.

The case was a second bug behind the words. The memory rail's heading carries `text-transform: uppercase`, which inherits, so a table that said `ok` reached the reader as `OK` and `halted` as `HALTED`. `.status` now sets `text-transform: none; letter-spacing: 0`, and the walk reads the computed `text-transform` of every chip it finds, so a container cannot shout a status again.

What is *not* a status is written down with its reason instead of being quietly tolerated: `PRD`, `MTP`, `CPU`, `RAM`, `PINNED`, `ESC`, `VIEW`, `USER TASK`, the counts (`0 / 0 Passed`), the model-residency chips (`LOADED`/`LOADING` - a property of a resource, not a state of a run) and the provider-route label `Unavailable provider · alias`. The inventory fails when a status position draws a word that is neither in the table nor in that list, so every exception has to be argued for.

The rule is checkable from both sides: `scripts/uiux_terminology_inventory.py` reads the table out of the source and finds any pane that still spells its own word or draws a word in the wrong tone, while `scripts/terminology_walk.mjs` opens each pane with that pane's own keyboard shortcut (Alt+1…Alt+6, read from the rail) and reads every status word the DOM actually holds - text, tone, and the computed case of the box.

An unknown state keeps the server's word. Mapping `something_new` onto `failed` or `ready` would be the pane asserting a fact it does not have; printing `something new` is ugly and true.

The stepper keeps one line and scrolls. Wrapping five stages into two rows would reorder the reading of a pipeline, which is worse than a horizontal scroll that the walk names.

evidence: Cost measured before changing anything, in the pane, on the demo fixture: `renderChatMessages()` took 1.64 ms with 2 messages, 5.01 ms with 20 and 11.98 ms with 60 (660 nodes); `renderStoredHarnessEvents()` took 0.40 ms with 40 events, 1.84 ms with 200 and 3.54 ms with 800 (2,970 nodes). Both grew with the session, which is the defect: a 400-token answer at 60 messages spent about five seconds of main-thread work on frames the reader never saw.

Root causes found by profiling rather than reading: a token rebuilt the HTML of every message (`renderMarkdown` over the whole transcript), and the harness render sorted all 5,000 cached keys plus merged and re-sorted the whole log before drawing a card - the profiler put 114.6 ms of a 20-frame burst in `getBoundingClientRect`, then 11.5 ms a frame in the render itself once the sort was gone.

known_regressions: A five-message conversation still pays about 0.7 ms a frame, and a 60-message one about 1 ms: that is the cost of drawing the message being written and it is not hidden.

Once the window is full, an arrival that is not a pure append (an approval changed, a gap forced a resync) still rebuilds the visible window at about 1.5 ms - a bounded cost, paid only when the cards on screen really did change.

The DOM now shows the newest 300 cards and not the whole log. The pane says so, the timeline count names the true total, Replay re-reads everything from the server, and the durable log, cursor and `retained_from_seq` semantics are untouched - but a reader looking for event 4,000 of 5,000 has to use Replay.

The client cache keeps 5,000 events, so a backgrounded tab that returns after more than 5,000 events gets a window rather than the whole log; the gap detection already forced a snapshot reload before this story and still does.

#185 is resolved by Option A: every strip and window-note headline names this view or its bounded 5,000-event cache, never the durable log's size. A smaller cache says how many last-reported events it holds; entries that outlived a server prune are explicitly outside the log's reported retained range and view-only. The owning walk exercises both cache/log directions and retains the #183 count == cards assertion after a pruned resync; its four captures are regenerated by the walk.

Carried forward: demo tok/s written to `perf_samples`; `ttft` fixture-equal; `prefill_tps`/`cached_tokens` unprinted; restored checkpoint carries no contract; Hall readiness refresh rewrites seat pickers; `auto_unload` drops just-compared model; browser comparison copy capped at 60,000 chars; `stopped` status carries warn tone; model-residency chips outside the vocabulary; `#chatMessages` stays `aria-live="off"` with its reason declared.
decisions: Coalesce by frame, not by timer: `requestAnimationFrame` is the unit the screen actually paints in, and a timer would either render work nobody sees or starve the last frame of a burst. The terminal frames bypass the queue because the frame that ends a turn is the one the reader is waiting for.

Compare shape, not content, to decide the cheap path. Hashing or diffing the transcript would cost as much as drawing it; the shape is six cheap facts per turn and it fails closed - any change it does not understand falls back to a full render.

Bound what is drawn (300 cards) and what is kept (5,000 events) at different sizes, because they answer different questions: what one screen can show, and how far back a scroll should reach without a fetch.

Say the window out loud rather than hiding it. A bounded DOM that does not admit it is bounded is a silent truncation; the note names the window, the count names the total and Replay names the way back.

Append only when the run on screen is still a contiguous run of the new window and no approval state moved. The approval rule is not an optimisation detail: those cards are already drawn, so an append would leave two versions of one approval on screen.

Batch the height read and skip it entirely for a reader at the bottom. Measurement inside a removal loop is what the profiler found; a follower is going to the bottom regardless, so the heights are only needed by the reader who is reading.
The cache keeps its own ascending key list instead of sorting on read. That is a memory cost of one array and it removed the length of the log from the cost of drawing a window.

A drawn window belongs to one session and to one read of the log. Two sessions' logs both start at seq 1, so a window carried over from the session a reader left answered "already drawn" for cards that were not on screen, and a re-read can bring back events that belong before the drawn window, which no append can express. The plan now takes the session with the seqs, and a cache reset drops the window bookkeeping with it (#169, #170 fixed in #183).
tracking.handoff_note: P5-04 is done. `scripts/stream_perf_walk.mjs` is the part to reuse: it times a real streamed reply and synthetic bursts in-page, asserts a per-token and per-frame budget, and refuses to report a walk it did not perform. `product/M5_2_0_UIUX_Stream_Performance.json` states the contract - a render that drops the shape guard, rebuilds every message, draws the whole log, appends across an approval change, or sorts the cache on read fails the inventory before it reaches a pane.
tracking.next_action: Start UIUX-P5-05 from this commit; the per-frame budgets and the walk's in-page timing are the pattern to extend, and the bounded DOM means any new per-card content has to fit a 300-card window.

stories.description: Incrementally implement visual and interaction polish using current code as authoritative baseline.
stories.current_behavior: Measured, not read. `node scripts/polish_walk.mjs` walked the six panes against the seeded demo app and found, before anything changed: of the 51 control kinds it could see, 30 answered the pointer with nothing at all, 28 answered a press with nothing, and 49 of the 53 focusable kinds drew no ring on keyboard focus. The primary action was the worst case - `.btn-primary, .btn-primary:hover:not(:disabled)` was one rule that re-declared the resting fill, so the one button a pane wants pressed was the one with no hover. Every corner was a hand-typed number (108 `border-radius` literals: 8px in 21 rules, 10px in 20, 7px in 18) and every duration was too (14: 150ms, 160ms, 120ms, 0.15s, 0.35s, 0.5s). 51/51 kinds was also wrong as a denominator: a checkbox is pressed through its `label`, and the walk was blind to it.
stories.target_behavior: One affordance for anything a reader can press, on a token scale. Pointing at a control changes something visible that is not movement; pressing it moves the surface; every focusable control draws the shared ring; a control that will not answer says so; and every corner and duration reads a token so the layer can be checked rather than described.

stories.current_behavior: Measured, not read. The ledger carried a 21-row feature-preservation matrix and the program had 17 browser walks, and nothing joined them: each story proved its own slice, no command ran the slices together, and no file recorded what happened when it did. A row could lose its proof without anything noticing - a reworded check title, a renamed test, an unmounted route or a button that lost its handler all failed silently as "preserved". A row that cannot be proved is reported as `known` with an issue behind it - never as a pass.

A worktree apply the server refused with 403 `Cannot apply worktree changes while session policy is read-only 'plan'.` printed "Applied!" in the ok tone and closed the diff dialog; a compaction on a session the server no longer had printed "Compaction checked."; a refused delete cleared the pane and re-read a list that still held the row; five MCP/OpenContext writes answered a refusal with `if (r.ok) { ... }` and nothing else. An attack on the running app found 12 refusals a write can meet across 9 statuses, and of the 35 mutating writes in the shell 17 had nothing between the click and the success path.
stories.target_behavior: A refusal is drawn as a refusal, where the action was, in the server's own words, with what was kept and a way forward - and never as an ok-tone success. It is proved by attacking the running app: 15 checks (16 with --screenshots) over refusals the server really produces (403 read-only, 404 gone, 401 wrong token and its recovery, 429 with Retry-After, a refused stream) and refusals a page cannot forge, injected at the network layer with app.py's own text; 0 page errors.

known_regressions: Carried forward unchanged from P6-01: demo tok/s, fixture-equal ttft, unprinted prefill_tps/cached_tokens, the checkpoint contract, Hall seat pickers, auto_unload, the 60,000-char copy cap, `stopped` warn tone, residency chips, `aria-live="off"`, the 5,000-event denominator.

The refusal is also announced as a toast with the server's reason (the inline box carries the actions). This is deliberate - a pane behind a backdrop or scrolled away still announces - but it means the same sentence can appear twice when the dialog is open.
decisions: The refusal is drawn where the action was. The apply control lives in the diff dialog, so the 403 is drawn inside that dialog and the dialog stays open - a refusal on the pane behind it is hidden from the reader who pressed the button, and the diff they were deciding on would vanish with it.

A guarded write returns null instead of a response, so a caller cannot fall through to its success path by forgetting a flag. That is why `if (!write) return;` is the first line after every guarded call, and why the success toast is below it.
A 429 is not offered a Retry that the server will refuse again: the control says `Retry in Ns`, is disabled, and re-enables itself as `Retry` when the server's own Retry-After expires.
The walk is written to fail on the pre-story code and that was checked by reverting the handler (12/16, `toasts: ok:Applied!`) - a check that cannot fail is not evidence.

The demo fixture cannot create a worktree session (`use_worktree: true` 500s on it), so the walk opens the diff dialog and reveals the Apply control a worktree session would show; the click, the request and the refusal are the app's own. The check says so rather than implying a worktree session existed.

Injected refusals are labelled `injected` in the walk and in the map with the reason the browser cannot produce them: a page cannot forge an Origin header, exceed the body limit without sending megabytes, or run a server with no token. The boundary's real contract is proved by the pytest nodes.
tracking.handoff_note: Every refusal now goes through refusalReader -> refuseWrite -> the shared presentation builder, and no caller can fall through to its success path, because guardedWrite returns null. Re-run `node scripts/adversarial_walk.mjs` (self-starting) after touching any write handler, and `python3 scripts/uiux_adversarial_inventory.py --check` after adding one: a new fetch() that never reads the status is a finding, not a style question.
